title: The household codes, honestly
hookLine: rules for wives, children and slaves reflect Roman households; churches read them in context
tomorrow: whose name comes first on the last page of Romans?

cards: Someone posts a screenshot of a Bible verse with one word underneath: yikes. The verse: "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord."

A little further down the same page it gets harder: "Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh." Closing the book right there is an honest reaction. So is reading the whole page.

teach.b: Readers call these passages household codes.
They sit in Colossians and Ephesians, and they walk through a household of the Roman world: husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and the slaves the King James calls servants.
The letters speak into that household as it was. They also lean on it.

teach.h: ONE TO ANOTHER, AND A MASTER ABOVE.
teach.b: Ephesians opens the section with everyone at once: "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God."
Then it asks a great deal of husbands: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it."
Colossians turns to masters: "give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven."

teach.h: TWO READINGS, EACH AT ITS BEST.
teach.b: Now two readings, each in its best light.
Some churches read the call to wives as a lasting pattern for marriage, rooted in Christ and the church, not in Rome, and always joined to a husband's self-giving love.
Others read it as part of a Roman household the gospel was already loosening, with one to another as the key. On slavery, history wasn't neat. People defending slavery quoted these verses.

People working to end it, Christians among them, quoted Galatians, "there is neither bond nor free," and Philemon, where a runaway is sent back "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved."

how: Churches read the household codes in worship and in Bible study, and they teach them differently: some as a lasting pattern for marriage and family, others as words for a Roman household read through 'one to another.'

o: the laws Moses gave for building a house
secret rules for keeping a family's money safe
lists of duties for each member of a Roman household

games.q: the household codes — tap the pairs.
p: a runaway returned as a brother

s: the household codes only give orders to wives, children and slaves
they speak to husbands, parents and masters too: love as Christ loved, be just, you also have a Master.
where the King James says 'servants' here, the Greek means slaves
the word is doulos; the codes speak to the slaves of a Roman household.
Paul also wrote 'there is neither bond nor free'
Galatians 3:28: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.

games.q: at youth group, two friends argue about Ephesians 5. one calls it a lasting pattern for marriage; the other says it was for a Roman household. you're asked for the best case of the side you don't hold. which is fair to the 'lasting pattern' side?
o: it's rooted in Christ and the church, and joined to a husband's self-giving love.
it means husbands simply matter more than wives do.
Rome required it, so it must still apply today.
games.why: readers who hold the lasting-pattern view root it in Christ's love for the church; readers on the other side point to 'one to another' as the key. stating each side at its best is how the two can keep talking.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who is still unfree today: someone in prison, someone trapped in work they can't leave, someone held by another person.
Keep them company in your mind for the length of the sit, by name or as a crowd, and if you pray, you can pray for them there.

wordCard.voice: The household codes. Lists in Colossians and Ephesians for wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters, spoken into a Roman household.

orig.note: Greek: a slave, a bondservant. The King James often renders it "servant."

carryVoice: Hold onto this: read in context, the codes speaking to their own world and pushing on it too. Go gently.
